title: Train to New York with the bass; uncle the pullman porter and Petrillo
summary: Jones and John Levy rode the 20th Century to New York; his uncle Benjamin Young, a porter, knew Petrillo and warned of the recording strike.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: But they were some very happy days. Very, very happy days. And -- oh, I'm trying to think when John Levy and I first went to New York. There were a lot of people that came to greet us at the railroad station, you know. And John lost his ticket, or somebody lost it for him. Because we came in a very first class train, you know. We had roomettes. But he had to put his bass in there. So he had to sleep -- he'd sleep in one bed and the bass would sleep in the other, you know? Oh, we made out all right, you know. But that was like what they called the crack trains in those days, because I had an uncle that was a pullman porter and a waiter on the 20th Century, the New York Central.
And he was there, oh, until he retired, you know.
You just remembered your uncle's name, I think, right?
Yeah. Benjamin Young. And he got to be

great friends with James Petrillo because Petrillo was the President of the Federation at that time. And that was just before the recording strike, and my uncle kept warning me to watch out for it, because Petrillo didn't like the recorded music that was featured in the -- oh, I think in the lounge, you know.
